title: Teacher Workflow No. 08 Your Reading Quiz Is Grading Who Read the
author: Winkel, Doan
summary: Author: Doan Winkel Source: How to Teach With AI (howtoteachwithai.substack.com), November 9, 2026 Category: Education - Ed-Tech URL: https://howtoteachwithai.substack.com/p/teacher-workflow-no-08-your-reading Doan Winkel points out that a weekly reading quiz built on main arguments and key terms now mostly measures who read an AI summary, since a summary can answer those questions. His workflow asks where, not what: NotebookLM generates questions anchored to specific places in the chapter, and a chatbot that has never seen the reading attempts them. Any question the chatbot can answer is cut, and the survivors are checked against the cited locations and assembled into a three-minute, reading-open, notes-closed card for the start of class. He keeps the check ungraded, so it stays a reading prompt instead of something to dispute, and tallies only patterns such as blank cards and where in the reading the misses cluster. The post ends with a ten-minute minimal version and a clear picture of how the class changes if you run it or skip it.
points: Questions about the main argument or key terms can be answered from an AI summary, so they test who read the summary and not who read the chapter.
Anchoring questions to a place in the text (a section, the sentence before a table) makes them depend on the pages being open.
Running the questions past a chatbot with no file, and cutting any it answers, is the step that stops you trusting the generated set.
Keeping the check ungraded and tallying patterns, not scores, reveals whether the reading load is too long without punishing students.
quotes: The reading quiz measures who read the summary. A summary tells a student what the author argues. It can’t tell them which section the author admits the exception in, or what sentence sits right before the table, or what example follows the claim in section three.
Scores went up, because the quiz is easier to pass from a summary than from the chapter, and the summary is one prompt away.
The tool likes to anchor a question to the page where an idea is explained instead of the page where it’s used.
Every question the chatbot gets right, or close enough that you’d give half credit, gets cut. A chatbot with no chapter answered it, so a student with a summary can too.
A student who read the chapter flips straight to the section. A student who read the summary is paging through a chapter they’ve never seen, and three minutes is not enough.
No points. The minute it’s worth points, the card becomes a thing to dispute instead of a thing to read.
By week four the blank count tells you more about your reading load than December’s evals will. Misses that always cluster past page ten mean the assignment is too long, and that fix is yours.
